text: You just saw how you can turn a requirement into a rubric.

You gave the judge a role, criteria, inputs, examples,
and output instructions,

but a clear-looking rubric does not guarantee that a judge
will apply it correctly.

Before you use its labels to decide what needs improving,
you need to test whether those labels can be trusted.
Let's go back to the shelter's safe matching evaluator.

The judge reads a volunteer profile, a dog record, and the agent's
recommendation, and it returns a label like SAFE or UNSAFE.

That label may look definitive, but it is still the judge's
interpretation of the rubric.
So you should treat the judge like a classifier.

It's assigning labels to cases, and you can test those labels by
comparing them with the reviewed labels from your benchmark.

When you do that, start with cases that weren't used to
write or tune the rubric.

If you test only on the examples you used while building the rubric,
the results can look better than they really are.

Those examples already shaped the evaluator.
So instead, keep a separate held-out set.

These are reviewed cases that the judge has not seen as prompt
examples, and that haven't been used to refine the rubric.

Run the judge on those held-out cases, and, for each case,
compare the judge's label with the reviewed label.

Suppose the shelter agent recommends a dog that requires an
experienced handler to a first-time volunteer.

A human reviewer labels that recommendation UNSAFE,
but the judge labels it SAFE. Now you have a disagreement.
the judge missed a failure that the reviewer caught.

Across the validation set, these matches and disagreements tell you
how reliably the judge is applying the rubric.

There are two useful metrics when measuring a judge's reliability:
precision and recall.

For this evaluator, focus on the UNSAFE label because unsafe
recommendations are the failures you most need the judge to catch.

Precision tells you of the recommendations that the
judge labeled UNSAFE,
how many were actually UNSAFE according to the reviewed labels?

If the judge labels a SAFE match as UNSAFE, that's a false alarm
that will cause precision to go down.
So precision tells you how often the judge's warnings are right.

Recall measures: of all the recommendations reviewers labeled unsafe,
how many did the judge catch?

If the judge labels an unsafe match as safe, that's a missed failure,
and it will bring recall down.

So recall tells you whether unsafe recommendations are slipping
through. Which mistake matters more depends on the requirement.

At the shelter, a false alarm means someone may review a safe
recommendation unnecessarily. That costs time.

But a missed failure means an unsafe match may move forward,
which could put a volunteer or a dog at risk.
So for the safe matching evaluator, recall matters a lot.

You may be willing to accept some extra false alarms if that helps
catch more unsafe matches.

One thing to note, recall and precision metrics are at
odds with each other.

If one goes up, the other goes down, so you can't prioritize both at
the same time. Another evaluator might need a different balance.

For example, if a judge flags too many acceptable responses for manual
review, it may become too noisy to use.

So don't treat precision and recall as abstract scores.
Read them in terms of what errors would actually cost.
You can also measure agreement across all labels with Cohen's kappa.

Imagine you've just reviewed 10 shelter cases,
nine of which you manually labeled as SAFE and one as UNSAFE.

Let's say the judge labels every case safe.
It agrees with the reviewer 9 out of 10 times.

That sounds like 90% agreement, but the judge missed the only unsafe
case. It didn't show that it can distinguish safe from unsafe matches.
It basically just benefited from choosing the most common label.

Cohen's kappa adjusts for the agreement you would expect by chance,
given how often the labels appear.
A kappa of 1 means the judge and reviewers matched on every label.

A kappa of 0 means their agreement was no better than chance, and a
negative kappa means they disagreed more than chance would predict.

Kappa is useful because it gives you a broader view of agreement,
but it's not enough by itself.

On a small validation set, one disagreement can move the score a lot.
And kappa only compares two sets of labels.

It doesn't prove that either label is correct.
The judge and reviewer can agree and still both be wrong.

Perhaps the reviewer missed an important detail,
or the rubric itself is unclear,
or maybe everyone is applying the wrong standard consistently.

So use the metrics as signals, not as the final answer.
When the labels disagree, inspect the case.

Read the volunteer profile, the dog record, and the agent's
recommendation, and go through the judge's explanation.
Then apply the safe matching requirement yourself.

If the judge's decision follows the requirement,
the reviewed label may need to be corrected.

If the reviewed label is right, the judge may have
misapplied the rubric.

And if the case could reasonably go either way,
the rubric might not be making the boundary clear enough.

A disagreement does not automatically mean fix the judge.
It tells you where the evaluation needs investigation.

As you inspect disagreements, look for patterns because some judge
errors are not random.

For example, suppose the agent recommends a calm senior dog to an
experienced volunteer. The response sounds careful.

It says the dog is gentle and explains that the volunteer has
handled many dogs before.

At first glance, the recommendation may seem safe, but the volunteer's
profile says they can safely handle dogs up to 50 lb.

This dog weighs 80 lb. So the problem is that the recommendation
ignores a physical handling limit.

An LLM judge might miss that if it focuses on the positive language
in the recommendation,

instead of comparing the dog's weight with the
volunteer's stated limit.

To see whether that mistake is part of a pattern,
compare similar cases.

Does the judge catch unsafe matches when the behavior risk is obvious,
but miss cases where the risk is a numeric constraint?

Or maybe recall drops when the recommendation sounds thoughtful
and the dog seems calm.

If so, the judge may be giving too much weight to the agent's
explanation and not enough weight to the underlying evidence.
One thing you can do is to try a targeted rubric change.

For example, before assigning a label, require the judge to identify
the volunteer's handling limit and the dog's weight,
then compare them directly.

That pushes the judge towards the evidence that should determine
the safety decision.
But don't assume the change helps just because it fixes one case.

Change one thing at a time, then test the revised rubric on
fresh reviewed cases.

If you use a disagreement to revise the rubric,
that case has now influenced the evaluator,
It's no longer a clean validation case for the revised version.

So when possible, test the revision on other reviewed cases that were
not used to make the change. Compare the old and new versions.

Did recall improve on unsafe matches?
Did precision fall too far? Did kappa improve?

Do the explanations show that the judge is using the relevant
volunteer and dog information?
Keep the change only if the evaluator improved overall.

If the change fixes one case but creates new errors elsewhere,
revise again or return to the previous version.

This is the same discipline you'd use when changing application code.
A local fix is not enough.

You need to know whether the change improves behavior across
the cases that matter.

So before you trust an LLM judge, bring several checks together.
Use recall to see whether it catches the failures you care about.

Check precision to see whether its warnings are usually right, and get
Cohen's kappa to measure agreement with reviewed labels beyond chance.
Inspect any disagreements to understand what actually went wrong.

and read explanations to confirm that the judge is applying the
requirement using the right evidence.

Only then should you rely on the judge's labels to guide
improvement or block a change.

using the dog shelter agent as an example.

You built a code evaluator when the requirement could
be checked strictly.

You chose an LLM judge when the requirement needed interpretation, and
you built a rubric to tell the judge how to apply that requirement.

And now you've seen how to test whether the judge's
labels are reliable.
